item.title: Trump's energy deal with Putin and Xi isn't sitting well with some Republicans
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Ukraine’s allies in Congress and across Europe were despondent Thursday, fearing that President Donald Trump’s latest gambit to increase global fuel supplies will weaken their effort to stop Russia’s aggression. Their concern followed a trilateral meeting in which Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping agreed to resolutions that included increasing energy output and condemning the International Criminal Court and “and other similar bodies” that have tried to hold Russia accountable for what United Nations investigators declared last month to be war crimes in Ukraine. Republicans in Congress called it a “big mistake” that won’t reduce fuel prices. “They use the proceeds of their exports to fund the war to kill Ukrainian civilians,” said Texas GOP Sen. John Cornyn , who is leaving the Senate after losing his primary in May. “I think that's a big mistake, and, also, I think it's the wrong cure for the disease because it really wasn't able to really have an impact on diesel prices before the midterms.” The White House says Trump’s intention is to help end the grinding war in Ukraine, but his critics in Congress and elsewhere see the agreement as empowering the Russian leader, who he called a “friend” at their summit in China and has frequently praised as a “genius.” Oleksandr Merezhko, a member of the Ukrainian parliament, described the meeting as “problematic” and said the optics were “unfortunate.” “Putin comes out ahead here, but only in terms of propaganda — there are no tangible results whatsoever,” Merezhko said. In Congress, multiple Republicans denounced the meeting, and the four-point joint statement issued by the U.S., China and Russia after the summit Thursday in Shenzhen. Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), a frequent Trump critic, said he hopes the incoming Democrats will hold the administration accountable in ways his own party didn’t. “If anybody is going to change it, it’s going to be a Democrat majority that will use leverage and I hope they do use whatever leverage they have to rescind the waivers,” Tillis said, referring to the president’s decision to waive sections of a new law that imposed tariffs on Russian oil and gas. Allowing a surge in Russian fuel products onto the market may end up “disincentivizing the development of refining capacity in the U.S.,” said Sen. Cynthia Lummis (R-Wyo.). White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said Trump is advocating for more oil on the market to lower gas prices and that his dealings with Putin do not detract from his desire to end the war in Ukraine. “President Trump is committed to achieving a lasting, just peace in Ukraine and ending the senseless killing,” she said. “The President has consistently advocated for more oil on the market to lower gas prices for American consumers; he continues to work to end the war in Ukraine while simultaneously putting America first.” Trump’s trilateral meeting came as his special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were in Berlin, meeting with European officials to seek a way to end the war. The president, on his way back to Washington, called into the meeting and said Putin was serious about negotiating a peace deal even as the Russian leader on Thursday denounced Ukraine’s strikes on the Crimean bridge , and vowed retaliation. “We will not negotiate. We will respond to these attacks,” Putin said, promising a response “much more painful” than the damage to the bridge. Still, Kushner and Witkoff, speaking after Trump’s call, insisted that peace was within reach and that the president was pushing toward that end. “The president has adamantly supported a peaceful end to this war,” Witkoff said. “And what I heard from him on the call today, was that he mentioned these very same principles to the other two leaders he was meeting with. He made Ukraine and a peaceful end to this a principle part of that trilateral today and I think needs to be commended for that.” The White House’s readout of the trilateral meeting didn’t mention Ukraine or a peace proposal. Nor did any of the leaders’ statements suggest that Trump pushed for an end to Putin’s aggression against Ukraine or challenged Xi’s role in supporting the conflict through exports of components essential to Moscow’s military. John Erath, who served as National Security Council deputy director for European affairs during the first Trump administration, said the trilateral meeting was aimed at achieving a short-term price dip in world markets with little concern for the broader geopolitical consequences. “Trump understands that an agreement — even a totally paper one — to increase energy supplies is going to have an effect on world markets and probably bring down the price of oil in the short term,” he said. “It’s geared towards the short-term movement in oil prices and what Americans pay at the pump, and I'm not sure there was much thought given for the long-term effects on Ukraine or elsewhere.” Gas prices have fallen significantly in recent weeks. The average price for a gallon of gas is $3.72, down from $4.30 one month ago. That drop is due in part to seasonal fluctuations as well as hopes for a negotiated end to the Iran war. On Thursday, energy markets had little reaction to the news out of the summit. Russia has little capacity to further relieve global energy prices after Ukraine destroyed or damaged 15 of its 35 refineries in recent months. November refinery volumes were cut almost in half, Reuters reported Wednesday , causing domestic fuel shortages and forcing a cut in some exports. U.S. officials have urged Kyiv to spare those refineries but Ukraine — and some of its European allies — have rejected stopping those strikes. Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby visited Brussels last week and admonished Ukraine for hitting oil and gas sites inside Russia, claiming they “have not been effective … nor do they contribute to blunting Russia’s advances on the front line.” NATO allies immediately pushed back with German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius calling Colby’s criticism “quite a stupid thing.” Veronika Melkozerova contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/19/trump-trilateral-backlash-republicans-ukraine-allies-01177262

item.title: Senate passes bipartisan bill to make data centers pay for their energy use
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Senate approved bipartisan legislation Thursday aimed at speeding up permitting reviews to build power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure as lawmakers seek to increase the nation’s energy supplies to meet surging demand and lower electricity prices. The legislation’s sweeping changes would shorten the timeline to start big energy projects and make sure data centers pay for the energy they use. Anger over data centers and rising electricity prices helped usher in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the energy-hungry behemoths. The 62-33 vote is the first major action by Congress since midterm elections that soundly repudiated President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans. The bill now goes to the House, which approved a more limited, industry-friendly version last year. The Senate bill would overhaul several environmental laws to make it easier to build energy infrastructure, drawing criticism from Democrats and environmental groups about limits on judicial review and changes to bedrock laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act. Trump urged approval of the bill, calling it a “BIG WIN for U.S. ENERGY INDEPENDENCE and DOMINANCE” in a recent social media post. The bill, formally known as the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026, will ensure the U.S. can build pipelines, mines and power plants more quickly, “lowering Energy Costs for American Families,” Trump wrote. Fifteen Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, voted for the bill. Two Republicans, Josh Hawley of Missouri and Mike Rounds of South Dakota, voted no. Industry groups back bill, but environmentalists fear it would weaken safeguards Major industry groups representing developers in clean energy and the oil and gas sector support the bill as a way to deliver more electricity to the grid and avoid delays for infrastructure projects that can stretch a decade or more. However, many environmental organizations have denounced the measure , saying it would lock in fossil fuel development, weaken environmental safeguards and make it harder for communities to challenge energy project approvals. “Make no mistake: This backroom deal will pave the way for even more fossil fuel projects like gas power plants for data centers, oil and gas pipelines and (liquefied natural gas) terminals while sacrificing fundamental and common-sense public health and environmental protections for communities across the U.S.,” said Jen Duggan, executive director of the Environmental Integrity Project. Benefits for renewable energy are outweighed by likely increases in greenhouse gas emissions and air and water pollution from the fossil fuel industry, Duggan and other critics said. She called the bill “a gift to some of the biggest polluters in America” and complained that it was being rushed through a lame-duck Congress without public hearings or sufficient debate. Democrats push for amendments A final vote on the measure was held up this week as Oregon's two Democratic senators pushed to add amendments, including one to ban data centers on public lands. Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden are among several Democrats in both chambers who say the party should use its stronger position in the next Congress to pass legislation that boosts clean energy, such as solar and wind power, while limiting expansion of oil, natural gas and other fossil fuels. “Getting more renewable electrons where they are needed doesn’t tackle climate change if you simultaneously promote the burning of more fossil fuels. Unfortunately, this bill does exactly that,” Merkley said. Majority Republicans stymied Merkley's effort to ensure votes on a host of amendments, including one that would block the Trump administration from continuing to cancel clean energy grants and other Democratic priorities for “purely political purposes.” The bill's sponsors reneged on promises of “a robust amendment process," he said. In the end, the measure was approved without amendments offered by rank-and-file senators. “I do think that this bill is very consequential to the future of this planet,” Merkley said. Major environmental groups, including the Sierra Club and National Wildlife Federation, oppose the bill, citing concerns about limits on judicial review and changes to the National Environmental Policy Act and other laws. The environmental policy law, known as NEPA, requires agencies to consider a project’s possible impacts and allows the public to be heard before a project is approved. The current review process often takes five years or more, and shortening that time frame is a key goal of the bill. “In America today, it takes too long and costs too much to build,” said Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso, the No. 2 Republican in the Senate. “Energy projects that would help lower prices remain frozen for years” as they await approval by the federal government. “Construction cannot start without first spending years in the regulatory penalty box,” driving up costs and creating uncertainty, Barrasso said. The bill’s four main champions — two Democrats and two Republicans — have released a detailed set of amendments designed to bolster support for the legislation. The four senators, who lead the chamber’s energy and environment panels, negotiated the deal a few weeks before the election. Republican Sens. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island say Americans are tired of paying more in utility bills while projects that could lower costs sit stuck in the planning phase for years. “We are going to make it easier to build in America again, and make life more affordable for American families,” Lee said. Co-sponsor calls bill ‘the floor, not the ceiling’ for legislative action on climate Whitehouse, a longtime climate hawk who has been criticized by some allies for supporting the permitting bill, said the measure is “the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations,” adding that he hopes “to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities” over the next two years. But Democratic Sen. Maria Cantwell of Washington state said the bill has been rushed and its impacts are not fully considered. Cantwell, who met Tuesday with tribal, outdoor recreation and conservation leaders, said the bill would undermine tribal nations and weaken protections for the nation’s bodies of water, land and wildlife. “Now is the time to slow this process down, to actually have a formal process” to debate and amend the bill, she said. “Don’t sacrifice the Clean Water Act or hunting or fishing grounds, historic or sacred sites, or protections of tribal sovereignty. We all need new sources of energy and power. But this bill, as it’s currently drafted, is not the answer.” Oneida Nation Vice Chairman Jameson Wilson said the bill threatens the tribe's ability to protect its sacred spaces, ancestors, traditional ceremonies and culture. “Any effort to accelerate development must strengthen, not diminish and erode tribal sovereignty and meaningful consultation,” he said. Former Energy Secretary Jennifer Granholm, who led the agency in the Biden administration, said she understands those concerns, but believes recent changes by bill sponsors strengthen protections for tribal consultation and restore important state authority over water quality. “A bigger Democratic majority can write a stronger bill,” Granholm wrote in a social media post. “But it would still need this president’s signature.” Sen. Alex Padilla, a California Democrat, said he supports and even authored many provisions in the bill, such as streamlining transmission infrastructure. But he voted no because the bill contains provisions he said would “irreparably harm California and the 109 federally recognized tribes who call California home.” He said he cannot sacrifice the rights of tribal governments or California’s environment. ___ Associated Press writer Jennifer McDermott contributed from Providence, Rhode Island. This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/senate-vote-bill-speed-permitting-020439514.html

item.title: DOJ ditches lawsuit that sought to pause certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate election
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in early 2026. (Photo by Eric Lee/Getty Images) Attorneys representing the U.S. Department of Justice told the federal 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday that they are no longer pursuing a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections over its handling of the state’s U.S. Senate election. In a new filing , attorneys for the federal agency said “this case has become moot,” a statement signaling they will not oppose the state certifying Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as the winner of the election. On Wednesday, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher said she intends to certify the election , including Peltola’s victory over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, next week. According to preliminary results through Wednesday, Peltola’s margin over Sullivan is greater than the number of first-choice votes cast for Sullivan and all other candidates combined. When seated in Congress, she will join a 56-person Democratic Senate majority elected amid a nationwide surge of support for Democratic candidates. Last month, the federal government, at the urging of President Donald Trump, sued the state and asked a federal judge to issue an order that would preclude elections officials from certifying Peltola as the election winner while it investigated whether the presence of independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan confused Alaska voters. Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit , saying the federal government lacked standing, but the Department of Justice appealed to the 9th Circuit. The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the national organization Common Cause, arguing on the appeal, asked the appellate court to issue a summary order upholding Gleason’s decision and asked the appellate judges to punish the federal attorneys that filed the case. “The legal theory advanced by the United States here is embarrassing and indefensible,” wrote attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union, which represented the two groups. “The Court should summarily affirm and then order the attorneys for the United States to explain why they or their client should not be sanctioned for pursuing a frivolous appeal.” On Thursday, the federal government responded, saying that instead of summarily upholding Gleason’s decision, the appeals court should vacate it, erasing it from the books entirely, because it is now moot. Alaskans have now voted, the federal government said, and ballots for Dan J. Sullivan are mixed with other ballots, making it impossible to determine who voted for Dan J. Sullivan. “The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,” the federal attorneys wrote. In late October, the New York Times reported that Dan J. Sullivan had been recruited by Democratic campaigners who sought to spoil the re-election campaign of Sen. Dan Sullivan. “The purpose of this lawsuit,” federal attorneys wrote, “was always to make sure that voters had the opportunity to cast a vote accurately reflecting their choice of candidate, notwithstanding the confusion caused (and intended to be caused) by Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign, egged on by Peltola’s.” While the civil lawsuit is winding down, a separate criminal investigation is continuing. The Anchorage Daily News reported on Wednesday that both the Alaska Bureau of Investigation and FBI are continuing to investigate whether any laws were violated by Dan J. Sullivan’s recruitment as a candidate. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. This article originally appeared on Alaska Beacon at https://alaskabeacon.com/2026/11/19/doj-abandons-lawsuit-that-sought-to-pause-certification-of-alaskas-us-senate-election/

item.title: Almost all of Anthropic's employees are now millionaires
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Anthropic captured a $1.76 trillion valuation on its first day of trading on the Nasdaq. - Mike Segar/Reuters Anthropic’s stock market debut turned the vast majority of the young startup’s staff into overnight millionaires — some many times over. The company’s headcount stood at 5,300 as of September this year, according to regulatory filings. After Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, about 600 employees entered the rarefied “centi-millionaire” club, with equity holdings valued north of $100 million, according to data from Hill.com , which tracks private-company shares. As many as 2,800 staffers, known internally as “Ants,” have holdings valued above $10 million. And about 5,100 — 96% of the staff — are sitting on equity north of $1 million. “What’s most surprising here is how quickly this this happened,” Andrew Benson, Hill’s founder and CEO, told CNN on Thursday, noting Anthropic has seen very little attrition. “It’s been pretty clear for some time that Anthropic is a rocket ship, and so it definitely discouraged people from leaving because they knew what the opportunity cost of that would be.” It’s not unusual for Silicon Valley startups, which are typically light on cash, to pay their staff with a combination of salary and stock. The promise of a future acquisition or initial public offering tends to keep workers motivated to work hard and stick it out until payday. But few startups have grown as big or as quickly as Anthropic. The company, founded in 2021, had fewer than 1,000 employees at the end of 2024. As with most tech startups, Benson noted, “being early is more important, in terms of a financial outcome, than being senior … You could be very low on the totem pole, and if you joined in 2023 or 2024, you’re likely to have a significantly better outcome than a senior person who joined earlier this year.” SpaceX, by contrast, spent more than two decades as a private company before its blockbuster IPO in June. That debut minted around 4,400 millionaires, out of a staff of 22,000. unknown content item - Anthropic’s IPO is also unique for allowing non-founder insiders to cash out on Day One of trading. In most IPOs, staff are subject to a “lockup” period — typically three to six months — during which they can’t sell their shares. But Anthropic’s listing included a complex, staggered lockup schedule that allowed non-founder insiders to cash out up to 10% of their shares as soon as the stock began trading. (It’s not known how many insiders may have taken advantage of the opportunity Thursday.) And unlike SpaceX, which has employees spread across Texas, California and Florida, Anthropic is uniquely concentrated in San Francisco, a city whose entire economy has been reshaped by sudden surges of tech wealth. A rash of newly minted millionaires could soon amplify pressure on San Francisco’s housing market, where home prices are already rising at their fastest pace in years. The typical home there sold for $1.7 million in October, up nearly 19% from a year earlier, according to Redfin. By contrast, the national median home price was roughly flat over the same period, at $416,700, according to the National Association of Realtors. CNN’s Samantha Delouya contributed reporting. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN Business at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/19/tech/anthropic-employees-now-millionaires

By Patricia Zengerle WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - US Senate Republicans on Thursday rejected legislation directing President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or obtain Congress' approval to continue, backing the president weeks ‌after sweeping defeats in midterm elections largely tied to Americans' frustration with the conflict. The Senate voted 51 ‌to 48, largely along party lines, to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House of Representatives. The US Constitution says that ​only Congress, not the president, can declare war, and Democrats have argued that Trump may have pulled the country into a long conflict by failing to spell out a clear strategy. Only three Republicans - Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky - voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution. One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted with ‌Republicans against it. The vote was the first ⁠on the conflict since Democratic victories in the midterm elections on November 3. Trump's fellow Republicans, who rarely break with the president, stood behind him in support of the US-Israeli war ⁠on Iran that started on February 28. Just 31% of Americans approve of the US war on Iran, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted November 13-16. It was the 21st vote in Congress on a war powers resolution since the war began. Democrats said ​they filed ​the measure to put Republicans on the record as supporting ​the war. SHOWDOWN LOOMS IN 2027 Democrats will control large ‌majorities in the House and Senate next year, and party leaders have pledged to make ending the war a top priority once they take over on January 3, setting the stage for a potential showdown with Trump. Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has called repeatedly for Congress to take back its control over declarations of war, said the midterm election result reflected Americans' unhappiness about the war, and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to ‌the conflict. "Its unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election ​results of November 3," Kaine said in a speech before the vote ​appealing for yes votes. Democrats made affordability a theme ​of the election campaign. Democrats have also balked at the cost of the foreign conflict, at a ‌time when Republicans have been cutting domestic programs ​like health insurance subsidies and ​free school lunches. Pentagon data in late October showed that the US military had spent over $47 billion to prosecute the war, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July. The latest resolution had passed the ​House in mid-September by 220-204, reflecting lawmakers' ‌growing unhappiness with the months-long conflict weeks before the midterms. A similar measure passed both the Senate and ​House earlier this year, but the Trump administration ignored it, saying it was not legally binding. (Reporting ​by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/us-senate-rejects-resolution-curbing-195349892.html

item.title: California State Bar opens investigation into former White House press secretary
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia, right, joins President Trump as he departs on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images) The State Bar of California has opened an investigation into Katie Zacharia, who faced scrutiny during her brief stint as White House press secretary for calling herself a lawyer despite never passing a bar exam. The probe, which was made public on Thursday, comes in response to a complaint submitted last month by the nonprofit watchdog Campaign for Accountability alleging that Zacharia may have violated California law by touting herself as lawyer. While Zacharia, a Huntington Beach native, received a law degree from Pepperdine University in 2011, she did not pass the bar exam in California or any other state. Yet, since at least early 2025 she has described herself as a lawyer on national television and in podcasts, including on “The Greg Kelly Show” and CNN, and has been identified on screen as a lawyer in at least 18 appearances on Fox News, according to the complaint. “Ms. Zacharia has represented herself as a lawyer repeatedly to buttress her reputation and credibility as a television legal commentator and now as the White House spokesperson, yet it seems it was all a lie. In California, calling yourself a lawyer without a license isn’t puffery; it’s a crime,” the organization’s executive director Michelle Kuppersmith said in a news release last month. Read more: Questions swirl about new White House press secretary's resume The watchdog’s complaint alleges Zacharia claimed to have served as “outside counsel” to the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation, and previously listed herself on LinkedIn as full-time General Counsel of Fix California, a nonprofit. A spokesperson for Zacharia denied that she had violated any laws in a text message to The Times, calling the accusations “baseless.” “This complaint is politically motivated and a clear waste of the State Bar’s time and resources. We are confident it will be dismissed with no finding of wrongdoing,” the spokesperson said. Under California state law a person presenting themselves as being entitled to practice law without an active state bar license could be charged with a misdemeanor and face up to a year in county jail and a $1,000 fine. Read more: White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia is leaving the job after a rocky start Zacharia addressed the scrutiny last month in an interview with conservative outlet Human Events, saying she had been preparing to take the bar exam in California shortly after getting married and was busy preparing for a move to China to join her new husband, who had been working in private equity in Beijing. “I was obviously incredibly distracted and overwhelmed and excited for finally being married to someone who I’d been long distance from for at least a year,” Zacharia told the outlet, adding that the results of the exam were “somewhat inconsequential” because she knew she would not need the credential in China. She said she had consulted several legal experts to ensure the title of lawyer was accurate when offering legal analysis and “they said absolutely, absolutely across the board. You can call yourself a lawyer,” she told the outlet. Zacharia added that it was “unfortunate that people dub this as some kind of conspiracy.” Times staff writer Clara Harter contributed to this report. Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/california-state-bar-opens-investigation-011152998.html

item.title: Trump says he still plans to meet Kim Jong Un after leaving Asia without talks
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Despite rumors about a surprise last-minute visit, President Trump clarified on Thursday that he did not meet North Korea's authoritarian leader Kim Jong Un on his way back from a whirlwind three-day trip to Asia that culminated in the first-ever trilateral summit between Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin . "The relationship is there, but we didn't meet," Trump told NBC News . "There was too many meetings [so] it wouldn't have worked out." But the president did vow to reconnect with Kim in the not-so-distant future. "We'll have that meeting at some point," he said. Earlier Thursday, the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries huddled for roughly 80 minutes in Shenzhen, China, before Trump departed for the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. The rumors about a possible stop in North Korea started when the traveling White House press corps reported that their phones had been " taken away" upon leaving China "for security reasons " — then intensified when social media users noticed that authorities had lifted a "temporary flight restriction" over Alaska that had been issued to allow Air Force One to land there for refueling. Pool reporters traveling with the President say that on departure, they were asked to hand over their phones (to US officials) for security reasons. This is very unusual. — Garrett Haake (@GarrettHaake) November 19, 2026 The fact that an unannounced presidential visit to the repressive communist state of North Korea seemed plausible reflects how Trump's relationship with Kim has evolved over the years. Initially, the dynamic between the two leaders seemed combative. They traded aggressive insults throughout 2017, with Trump mocking Kim as " Little Rocket Man " and Kim ridiculing Trump as a " mentally deranged U.S. dotard ." But Trump later said that letters from the North Korean leader softened his stance. "I was really being tough. And so was he. And we'd go back and forth. And then we fell in love," Trump said in 2018. "He wrote me beautiful letters. And they're great letters. We fell in love." Trump wound up meeting Kim three times during his first term: in Singapore in 2018; in Vietnam in 2019; and in the Korean Demilitarized Zone later the same year. Since then, North Korea has reportedly acquired more nuclear weapons and expanded the original uranium enrichment facility at its main nuclear complex — a "cause for serious concern," according to the United Nations' nuclear watchdog . Trump and administration figures had hinted that another encounter with Kim could be in the offing. Upon returning to the White House in January 2025, the president told Fox News that he would reach out to Kim again — and according to MS Now , "U.S. representatives at the U.N. tried several times to deliver a letter from Trump to Kim in the first months of Trump's term." The president told reporters Tuesday in the Philippines that Kim "would like to" meet in China. Trump is "prepared to do it," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the same day. "If we have a problem with North Korea, the only way we're ever going to solve it is if we engage with them." Rubio added that "the president has never viewed meeting and talking to someone as a concession." Kim previously signaled that he would be willing to talk if the U.S. dropped its "hostile policy" toward North Korea and respected what he calls its status as a nuclear state. Kim's goal, experts say, is to win international recognition as a nuclear state so it can push the U.N. to lift crippling economic sanctions. Before meeting Xi and Putin in China, Trump said discussing nuclear weapons was his top priority, and he insisted Thursday in his opening remarks that the three powers were "uniquely positioned" to reduce the number of nukes in the world. But a brief four-point statement issued after the summit offered only loose commitments to "engage in dialogue on reducing nuclear risks." Trump has long focused on the threat of nuclear weapons, often citing his uncle John G. Trump, a professor of engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as the source of his concern. "My uncle used to tell me about nuclear before nuclear was nuclear," Trump said in 2015 . "I hate nuclear more than any," he added the following year . "My uncle was a professor, was at MIT [and] he used to tell me about the problem." This article originally appeared on Yahoo News at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/article/trump-says-surprise-visit-with-north-koreas-kim-jong-un-on-asia-trip-didnt-work-out--but-vows-to-have-that-meeting-in-the-future-205124200.html

item.title: JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard disclose cyberattack on third-party vendors
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ), Visa ( V ), and Mastercard ( MA ) said on Thursday that some select customer data, including names and emails, was accessed by attackers after a cyberattack on a vendor. Spokespeople for the companies said no payments or card data was leaked and that their own systems were not affected by the incident. JPMorgan said it believes hackers who attacked a third-party vendor accessed marketing data, including customer names and email addresses. The bank also said the incident isn't related to outages many of its customers reported earlier this week, which it blamed on a software bug . "Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," a JPMorgan spokesperson said. "We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," a Mastercard spokesperson said. "There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," the person added. A Visa spokesperson added claims of the incident are associated to a third-party service provider in the Asia Pacific region. "This is unrelated to any of the system disruptions across different industries this past week," the Visa spokesperson added. A ransomware group known as n0n has claimed responsibility for the attacks on the dark web and shared sample data as proof, according to cybersecurity firm SOCRadar. The cybersecurity firm told Yahoo Finance that it hasn't independently verified whether the ransomware group carried out the intrusion. It also supported JPMorgan, Visa and Mastercard's statements that the breaches most likely originated at a third-party vendor and involved marketing and benefit-program data such as names and email addresses. "The most immediate risk for consumers is targeted phishing that impersonates their bank or card provider," SOCRadar chief information security officer Ensar Seker said in an emailed statement. The latest incident comes as consumers are on high alert after a string of major technology outages this November . The Wall Street Journal earlier reported the connection between the breaches and the ransomware group. Follow David Hollerith on X @DsHollers .
